analysis.one_liner: Balances the budget in seven years by cutting Medicare, Medicaid, welfare, and student loans while cutting taxes and selling federal resources.
analysis.headline: The House's 1995 balanced-budget reconciliation bill was referred to 15 committees and subcommittees but never received a vote, dying when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the House Republicans' omnibus bill to balance the federal budget over seven years. It would have restructured Medicare, replaced the Medicaid guarantee with capped block grants to states, enacted the House welfare bill, killed the federal Direct Loan student loan program, raised veterans' drug copays, and delayed federal retiree cost-of-living adjustments. To pay for a package that also cut capital gains taxes, it would have opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil leasing, sold federal ski areas and naval petroleum reserves, set a low royalty on hardrock mining, and given broadcasters digital TV licenses without auction.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and higher-income households, through lower capital gains and estate taxes and new medical savings accounts. Mining, oil, and grazing interests, through cheap access to federal lands and resources. Guaranteed student loan lenders, through the elimination of the competing federal Direct Loan program. Broadcasters, through free digital TV licenses. Banks, through lighter Community Reinvestment Act obligations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, lenders, miners, and energy firms

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the capital gains deduction for individuals from 50 percent to 34.5 percent and cuts the corporate alternative capital gains rate to 25 percent, plus estate and gift tax changes, under the Contract with America tax relief title.

Directs the Interior Department to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to competitive oil and gas leasing, declares existing environmental reviews legally sufficient, and authorizes exports of Alaskan North Slope oil.
Sets a 3.5 percent royalty on net proceeds for hardrock mining on federal land and issues mining patents at the fair market value of the land excluding the minerals in it.

Terminates the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan Program, ending the government's option to lend to students directly and steering all federal student lending back through banks and guarantee agencies.

Exempts banks with up to $100 million in assets from Community Reinvestment Act evaluations, allows qualifying institutions to self-certify compliance, and bars regulators from imposing additional CRA recordkeeping or data requirements.

Assigns new terrestrial digital television licenses to existing broadcast licensees outside the competitive bidding (auction) process, and requires auctioning at least 100 megahertz of other spectrum below three gigahertz.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income families who rely on Medicaid and welfare, seniors under a restructured Medicare, students losing the direct loan option and grace-period interest subsidies, veterans paying higher prescription copays, federal employees and retirees facing delayed cost-of-living adjustments, and taxpayers who would see federal lands and mineral rights transferred at bargain terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid and welfare recipients, seniors, students, veterans

drawbacks.text: The Medicaid title terminates the existing Medicaid program and replaces it with state block grants while expressly declaring that no individual has a federal entitlement to medical assistance and no person can sue a state in federal court over the plan — meaning coverage guarantees would depend entirely on state budget choices.

It raises the veterans' outpatient prescription drug copayment from $2 to $3 and terminates the Secretary's authority to waive it, and rounds veterans' disability compensation cost-of-living adjustments down to the next whole dollar.

It repeals the earned income tax credit for workers without children, raises phaseout rates, and counts Social Security and pension income against eligibility — reducing work support for low-wage childless workers.
It eliminates grace-period interest subsidies on new student loans and caps federal parent PLUS loans at $15,000 per student per year while raising their interest rates.

Even an honest supporter would acknowledge the design tension: the bill pursues deficit reduction while simultaneously cutting capital gains and estate taxes, so the savings come disproportionately from health care, welfare, and veterans' programs while the tax relief flows toward households with appreciated assets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Slowing deficit growth was a legitimate goal, and some provisions — the taxpayer rights protections, expanded VA eligibility for veterans exposed to toxic substances, and prosthetics access — are genuine improvements. But the bill's overall architecture moves money in one direction: tax relief skewed toward capital gains holders and estate planning, cheap federal resources for extractive industries, and protected market positions for lenders and broadcasters, financed by converting health coverage and income support for poor families into capped, discretionary block grants with no federal guarantee. Weighing it honestly, the costs to ordinary people are concrete and immediate while the benefits accrue mainly to concentrated interests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to 15 House committees, then split among nine subcommittees in early November 1995, and nothing further happened before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kasich of Ohio, chairman of the House Budget Committee, introduced the bill on October 20, 1995, as the reconciliation vehicle pursuant to the fiscal year 1996 budget resolution, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the Budget Committee plus 14 other committees covering agriculture, banking, commerce, education, the judiciary, resources, ways and means, and more.
On November 6, 1995, portions were referred to nine subcommittees across Commerce, Transportation, and other committees — the last action recorded.

The bill's titles would enact other House-passed bills into law directly, including the Medicare Preservation Act (H.R. 2425), the Personal Responsibility welfare bill (H.R. 4), and the Contract with America tax relief provisions of H.R. 1215.
No floor vote, committee vote, or further action appears in the record before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income families, seniors, students, and veterans kept the existing guarantee structures of Medicaid, student loans, and veterans' benefits, since the bill's cuts and block grants never advanced. The mining, oil, banking, ski, and broadcasting interests that stood to gain from the bill's resource transfers and deregulation gained nothing either. The broader seven-year budget fight it was part of ended without the House reconciliation package becoming law, and the era's major deficit fight concluded with the programs intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beneficiaries of Medicaid, welfare, and veterans' benefits

for.name: Rep. John Kasich
for.role: Chair, House Budget Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the omnibus reconciliation bill on October 20, 1995, drafting every committee's savings and tax provisions into a single vehicle to implement the seven-year balanced budget plan.

for.name: House Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Built the bill around the House-passed Medicare restructuring, welfare, and Contract with America tax bills, routing them through the reconciliation process that cannot be filibustered in the Senate.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed the congressional seven-year balanced budget plan built on these Medicare and Medicaid cuts and vetoed the companion reconciliation bill in December 1995, producing the budget standoff and government shutdowns of late 1995 and early 1996.

against.name: Congressional Democrats
against.role: Minority parties in the House and Senate
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Medicare and Medicaid restructuring and the size of the tax cuts in the 1995 budget reconciliation package, contributing to the package's failure to become law.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Republican leadership product with no cosponsors and no recorded votes; the broader 1995 budget battle split sharply by party, with Republicans pushing the seven-year balanced budget and Democrats, joined by President Clinton, blocking its enactment.

industries.note: The bill would charge a 3.5 percent royalty on net proceeds and allow patents at land value excluding the minerals, transferring federal mineral wealth at a fraction of what critics of the time considered market value. Ordinary taxpayers bear the difference as foregone public revenue.

It would open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to leasing with environmental reviews pre-declared sufficient, authorize North Slope oil exports, and order sale of naval petroleum reserves. Public lands and energy security would be converted into private extraction rights while Alaska receives half of federal revenues.

industries.industry: Guaranteed student loan lenders and guarantee agencies
industries.note: Terminating the Direct Loan program eliminates the cheaper government-run competitor and locks banks and guarantee agencies back in as the channel for federal student lending, with added fees and subsidies written into the bill. Students lose the direct loan option and grace-period subsidies.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare managed-care plans
industries.note: The bill enacts the House Medicare restructuring bill into law, shifting Medicare toward private plan competition, and converts Medicaid into capped state block grants with no federal individual entitlement. States and private plans become the permanent gatekeepers of coverage for low-income and elderly Americans, with the bill expressly barring federal lawsuits over state plan compliance.

The Community Reinvestment Act amendments exempt banks up to $100 million in assets, allow self-certification, and bar regulators from adding recordkeeping or data requirements, weakening the main lever communities have had to press banks to lend in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

Incumbent licensees would receive new terrestrial digital TV licenses outside the auction process — a public spectrum asset transferred to existing broadcasters at no charge, while other spectrum is auctioned.

The Freedom to Farm provisions replace price supports with seven-year fixed 'market transition' payments totaling about $38.7 billion through 2002, locking in direct subsidies regardless of prices or crop planted. This reduces market distortion but entrenches a guaranteed revenue stream to landowners, capped at $50,000 per person per year.

industries.industry: Ski area operators and federal grazing permit holders
industries.note: The bill would require offering at least 40 national forest ski areas for sale to their operators and establish 15-year grazing permits with a new fee formula. Both transfer long-term control of public land use to commercial users on favorable terms.
